Main Points
⏺ Upgradable contracts can change logic without changing the address — great for iteration, risky for trust
⏺ The risk is not only bugs, but who controls upgrades and keys
⏺ This post explains why upgrades can be the biggest protocol risk

1️⃣ Why Upgrades Exist — patch bugs, ship features, adjust parameters without forcing migrations.
2️⃣ How It Works — typically proxies: same address, changeable underlying logic.
3️⃣ Risk Surface — admin keys, multisig compromise, upgrade mistakes, permission abuse.
4️⃣ What To Look For — timelocks, transparent governance, audits of new versions, upgrade history.
5️⃣ Practical Lens — if a protocol is fully admin-controlled, treat it like fintech, not immutable “code-is-law.”

Final Thoughts

Upgradable means faster iteration — and more trust. Sometimes the biggest DeFi risk isn’t the code, it’s the right to change the code.

52–52, Until the Court Counts

Kan 11’s latest poll gives Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar! 23 seats and Likud 21. Netanyahu’s bloc and the “change” bloc each land on 52. The remaining 16 seats include 12 held by Ra’am and the Joint List, the same two Arab lists the Central Elections Committee has moved to remove from the ballot. 

The headline gap between Yashar! and Likud matters inside the opposition. Eisenkot, not Bennett, would lead its largest party. It does not change the government arithmetic. No bloc is near 61. The government depends on a handful of seats, the legal status of the Arab lists and the willingness of parties to sit with one another after election night.

On September 23, the Central Elections Committee voted 18–5, with one abstention, to bar Ra’am. The petitions came from Likud, Otzma Yehudit and the Choosing Life forum of bereaved families. The same 18–5 result barred the Joint List, which combines Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. The Attorney General’s Office opposed both bans, arguing that the evidence did not meet Israel’s demanding legal standard for disqualification. 

The committee also barred two individual candidates:

Hadash MK Ofer Cassif, by 19 votes to five with two abstentions. The committee accepted the Likud petition on the ground of alleged support for armed struggle. 

Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, by roughly 30 or 31 votes to four. Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, the committee chair, joined that vote, breaking the customary restraint of chairs in candidate-disqualification cases. 

The court must approve a ban on an individual candidate before it takes effect. Parties have to file their own appeals against a ban on their list. 

That procedural difference matters: Cassif and Abu Shehadeh reach the Supreme Court automatically; Ra’am and the Joint List must ask it to reverse the committee. 

If both lists are ultimately excluded, their seats do not vanish. The Knesset still has 120 seats, and the votes redistribute among lists that pass the 3.25 percent threshold.

A simple proportional redistribution puts each major bloc roughly five or six seats higher, still short of 61. Actual results would depend on Arab turnout, whether Arab voters move to the Democrats or another eligible list, and which smaller parties clear the threshold. 

Lower turnout also reduces the raw vote total needed to pass the threshold, raising the relative value of disciplined electorates, especially Haredi and religious-Zionist voters.

The political effect is stranger than the arithmetic. Ra’am can, at least in theory, help a change bloc reach a working arrangement. The Joint List cannot plausibly be the coalition partner of Bennett, Eisenkot and Liberman. Their 12 poll seats therefore look like one coalition resource only from a distance.

Disqualifying Ra’am and the Joint List would remove Likud’s favorite accusation: that the opposition intends to govern through Mansour Abbas. 

It would also remove an internal fracture inside the opposition, where Yair Golan is open to Arab participation while Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman reject it.

That gives the opposition a cleaner story: a Zionist cabinet of the center and moderate right. It especially helps Eisenkot, whose party leads the field but whose coalition has no natural path through the Arab lists.

Netanyahu gets a different benefit. The exclusion fight turns the campaign toward security, loyalty and representation. 

Even if the Supreme Court restores the lists, Likud can say the court enabled the coalition it warned about. If the bans stand, Arab turnout may fall and the right’s disciplined base becomes more valuable.

🔔 South Korea targets November review for second stage crypto legislation 

🌐 South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has set November for a National Assembly subcommittee review of the Digital Asset Framework Act, rejecting claims that work on the country’s second stage crypto legislation has been delayed. According to Seo Na yoon, head of the FSC’s virtual asset division, the regulator and lawmakers are moving in the same direction on legislation covering digital asset issuance and distribution, including stablecoins. Speaking at a National Assembly seminar in Seoul on Sept. 22, Seo said differences remain over when the government will submit its draft, but the November review remains part of the planned timetable. 

⚡️ “The FSC is not dragging its feet at all. We share the same view,” Seo said, responding to criticism over the pace of the legislation. “The direction has already been set, and while detailed discussions may be necessary in the process, there is certainly no intention on the FSC’s part to delay.”

🔗 Seo said the regulator wants the legislation passed quickly and expects discussions to proceed using bills that lawmakers have already introduced alongside the government’s proposal. Ten digital asset and stablecoin bills are currently pending in the National Assembly, giving lawmakers existing proposals to work from before the government completes its version.

Delaware Judge Orders Fox Corp. to Dump Hundreds of Files on Murdoch, Deleted Texts, Phone Hacking, and the Dominion Settlement In Massive Shareholder Lawsuit | Jim Hoft, The Gateway Pundit

A Delaware judge has just ordered Fox Corporation to hand over a mountain of internal records in a long-running shareholder lawsuit aimed at Rupert Murdoch, his son Lachlan, and other Fox directors. The files cover phone hacking, board minutes, emails, and the deletion of Rupert Murdoch’s text messages.

The order landed last week from Vice Chancellor Bonnie David. Fox fought to keep the material sealed. The judge sided with the plaintiffs across the board.

According to NPR, the haul includes roughly 700 documents that mention “phone hacking,” years of Fox board meeting minutes, emails from former Ford CEO and longtime Fox director Jacques Nasser’s Ford accounts, and a list of every email address ever used by Nasser or Rupert Murdoch.

Shareholders’ lawyers will also get sealed records from the still-pending Smartmatic case that deal with what the court calls Murdoch’s “spoliation” of records, legal speak for wiping texts.

The case was filed about three years ago by five New York City public-employee pension funds and Oregon’s public employee retirement system.

Those are Democrat-run, taxpayer-backed institutions using Delaware corporate law to try to pin Fox’s legal bills on the Murdochs personally.

The Associated Press reported earlier that the same funds accuse Murdoch and other Fox leaders of ignoring “red flags” after 2020.

The lawsuit was lit by Fox’s nearly $787.5 million settlement with Dominion Voting Systems in April 2023, one of the largest defamation payouts in American history. Smartmatic is still suing and wants $2.7 billion.

The Gateway Pundit said at the time that Fox rolled over. Joe Hoft wrote that the mainstream media was “giddy” and that Fox “gave the MSM everything they ever wanted.”

Harvard law professor Alan Dershowitz told The Gateway Pundit the Dominion deal “never should have happened” and that “something else had to have been involved.”

Bill O’Reilly said the same week that Rupert Murdoch settled because he did not want to take the stand. “He told his lawyers settle it,” O’Reilly said.

Now those same settlement dollars are being used as the launch pad for this derivative suit. The pension funds want the Murdochs and other directors to personally eat the loss.

Seth Rich Is Back in the File

The complaint also points to Fox’s retracted 2017 reporting on murdered DNC staffer Seth Rich and what plaintiffs call an undisclosed settlement with the Rich family. Fox published, then yanked, a story suggesting Rich may have leaked Democratic emails to WikiLeaks.

The Gateway Pundit has covered the Rich case for years. In 2018 we reported that a federal judge dismissed the Rich parents’ lawsuit against Fox News.

This summer TGP reported attorney Ty Clevenger’s claim that the FBI had stashed hundreds of Seth Rich pages in a previously hidden SCIF room at headquarters, mixed with burn bags.

The Left treated any question about Rich as forbidden. Fox folded the story. The pension-fund lawyers now want to use that episode as proof the board ran a “scandal business model.”

Phone Hacking and Wiped Texts

The British phone-hacking scandal at News Corp. titles more than a decade ago has already cost that side of the Murdoch empire an estimated $1.5 billion, according to NPR.

Fox Corp. was split off from News Corp. after that mess. Plaintiffs want the “phone hacking” paper trail anyway, plus board records from Fox and related companies.

Then there are the texts.

Fox’s own lawyer, Anitha Reddy, told the Delaware court that claims of wholesale deletion are “incorrect,” but she admitted “there was a period … when text messages were not retained.”

Court argument, as reported by NPR, is that Rupert Murdoch auto-deleted texts until about April 2022, after Dominion had already sued.

Shareholders now get the sealed Smartmatic file on that spoliation fight.
